drills.q: In one sentence each, what question do RBAC, ABAC, and ReBAC answer?
drills.a: RBAC: what may this job function do. ABAC: under what conditions. ReBAC: what relationship does this user have to this specific object.

drills.q: Write the Zanzibar tuple format and give one example with a userset subject.
drills.a: object#relation@subject. Example: doc:roadmap#viewer@group:eng#member -- the subject is itself a userset, so every member of group:eng is a viewer of doc:roadmap.

drills.q: Name the three logical components in NIST SP 800-207 and which two form the PDP.
drills.a: Policy Engine (decides), Policy Administrator (establishes or tears down the session credential), and Policy Enforcement Point (sits in the data path in front of every resource). PE + PA together form the PDP.

drills.q: Name the five pillars of the CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model v2.0 and its four maturity stages.
drills.a: Pillars: Identity, Devices, Networks, Applications and Workloads, Data. Plus three cross-cutting capabilities (Visibility and Analytics, Automation and Orchestration, Governance). Stages: Traditional, Initial, Advanced, Optimal. Published April 2023.

drills.q: A team has 3 job functions, 4 regions, 3 environments, and 2 data classifications, all encoded as roles. How many roles, and what do you actually do about it?
drills.a: 3 x 4 x 3 x 2 = 72 roles for one conceptual job function. The fix is not consolidating roles, it is moving the exploding dimensions out: region and environment become attribute conditions (or relationships if they are really resource scoping), and RBAC keeps only the genuinely static coarse function. Adding one more dimension multiplies again, which is why 'just add a role' is a trap.

drills.q: Your RLS policy is written, the table has ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, and every tenant still sees every row. Give three candidate causes in likelihood order.
drills.a: 1) The app connects as the table OWNER, and owners bypass RLS by default -- needs ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY plus separating the migration role from the runtime role. 2) The app role is superuser or has BYPASSRLS; the built-in postgres role has BYPASSRLS and it cannot be removed. 3) The policy reads a setting that was never set, so current_setting(..., true) returns NULL and the comparison is NULL rather than false.

drills.q: Explain why SET LOCAL matters for tenant context, and what exactly goes wrong with plain SET.
drills.a: SET is session-scoped and persists on the backend connection after the transaction ends. Under a pooler in transaction pooling mode (PgBouncer), the next request that borrows that connection inherits the previous tenant's context, so tenant A reads tenant B's rows. SET LOCAL (or set_config(name, value, true)) is transaction-scoped and is discarded at commit or rollback, so it cannot leak. It must be inside an EXPLICIT transaction to have any effect. Symptom signature: cross-tenant reads that appear only under load, because that is when connection reuse actually occurs.

drills.q: Reads are correctly tenant-scoped but rows are appearing under the wrong tenant_id. What is missing from the policy?
drills.a: WITH CHECK. USING filters reads and the pre-image of a write; WITH CHECK validates the post-image of INSERT and UPDATE. With only USING, an UPDATE ... SET tenant_id = <other tenant> passes because the row was visible before the change and nothing validates it after. Add WITH CHECK with the same predicate.

drills.q: Why can ABAC not power a sharing UI or a quarterly access review?
drills.a: Because access is computed, not stored. Answering 'who can access this document' requires evaluating the policy against every principal in the system, which is O(subjects). ReBAC answers the same question with an Expand over the userset tree, bounded by the actual relationship graph and typically tens of tuples. If a product manager will ever ask to display who has access, you need stored grants for at least that surface.

drills.q: Give both flavors of the new enemy problem and say what the zookie actually guarantees.
drills.a: Flavor 1, ACL updates out of order: remove Bob from the folder at t1, add a secret doc at t2; a replica applying t2 first lets Bob read it. Flavor 2, old ACL applied to new content: remove Bob from the doc at t1, add sensitive content at t2; if the content read is authorized against a pre-t1 ACL snapshot, Bob reads the new content under the old permission. The zookie is an opaque token carrying a Spanner timestamp recorded when content is written; a Check passing that zookie is guaranteed to evaluate at a snapshot no earlier than that timestamp. It preserves causal ordering between content and ACL updates while leaving Zanzibar free to choose any LATER timestamp, which is what keeps the cache hot enough for p95 under 10 ms at 4.2M Check QPS.

drills.q: Design tenant isolation for a SaaS going from 20 to 2,000 tenants. State the model, the enforcement, and the escape hatch.
drills.a: Silo does not survive: 2,000 databases means 2,000 migrations per release and a per-tenant cost floor that kills the low tier. Target pool with rungs 3 and 4: shared database with RLS plus FORCE, SET LOCAL inside an explicit transaction, tenant_id as the leading column of every composite index, and dynamically-scoped STS credentials at the compute layer so enforcement sits outside the process that has the bug. Build a bridge escape hatch NOW: a routing layer reading tenant metadata so contractually-isolated tenants get their own database or KMS key with an identical code path and only a different connection target. Budget separately for the surfaces RLS does not cover: cache keys, background jobs, search index, object storage. The sequencing point is that adding routing indirection at 20 tenants is a week and retrofitting it at 2,000 is a multi-quarter project.

drills.q: Argue why RLS is not a complete tenant-isolation boundary, with named CVEs.
drills.a: It is bypassed by superusers and BYPASSRLS roles (the built-in postgres role has BYPASSRLS and cannot have it removed), and it silently no-ops for table owners without FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY. It has had boundary CVEs: CVE-2024-10976, where incomplete tracking of RLS tables let a reused plan under a subquery, WITH query, security-invoker view, or SQL-language function return rows for the wrong user; and CVE-2025-8713 (14-Aug-2025, fixed in 17.6/16.10/15.14/14.19/13.22), where optimizer statistics -- histograms and most-common-values lists -- leaked sampled data RLS intended to hide via a crafted leaky operator. And it only covers Postgres: the cache, search index, object storage, and message queue are all outside it.

drills.q: Your centralized PDP is down. Fail open or fail closed? Defend the answer.
drills.a: Per action class, decided in advance and written down. Money movement, permission changes, and data export fail closed, always. Reads of non-sensitive data may serve from a decision cache with a bounded TTL. The two wrong answers are 'fail closed everywhere' without acknowledging you have made the PDP a single point of total outage, and 'fail open' without naming which specific actions you are willing to let through unauthorized. Not deciding is deciding, and it defaults to whatever the HTTP client's error handling does.

drills.q: Someone presents a completed zero trust rollout as remediation for your Broken Access Control findings. Respond.
drills.a: They are orthogonal. Zero trust is about the network and the session: mTLS, device posture, identity-aware proxies, per-session credentials. Object-level authorization is about the row. A fully zero-trust network still returns tenant B's document to tenant A when the handler fetches by id and never checks ownership, because the PEP authorized access to the SERVICE and A01/BOLA live entirely behind it. A01:2025 is #1 in the web Top 10 with 40 CWEs at 3.73% average incidence and API1:2023 BOLA is #1 in the API Top 10 precisely because these bugs survive every network control you can buy.

drills.q: You inherit a pool-model SaaS where tenant filtering is hand-written in every repository. Sequence the remediation and name the operational cost of step two.
drills.a: 1) Audit: query-log check in staging asserting every statement touching a tenant table carries a tenant predicate, so you have a count rather than a feeling. 2) Ship the enforcement rung that catches everything at once: RLS with FORCE, a tenant_scope context manager using SET LOCAL in an explicit transaction, and a fail-closed assertion when no tenant context is set. This converts every existing missing-predicate bug from a confidentiality failure into an empty result set. 3) Fix what RLS does not cover, in incident-frequency order: background jobs, cache keys, search index, object storage. 4) Two-tenant integration suite in CI asserting zero cross-tenant rows on every endpoint. 5) Only then remove the now-redundant hand-written predicates, and only where tests cover them. The operational cost of step two is a wave of tickets in week one as previously-silent bugs become loud empty responses -- staff for it, and treat each one as a found bug, not a regression. Failing toward availability instead of confidentiality is the correct direction.
